extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for forming and evaluating a prima facie case of obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103, including required factual findings, how to articulate rationale, and examples of acceptable lines of reasoning. Covers examiner duties to consider applicant evidence and to tie factual findings to the legal conclusion of obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for explicit, reasoned analysis supporting 35 U.S.C. 103 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: The analysis supporting a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 should be made explicit; rejections cannot be sustained with mere conclusory statements and must include articulated reasoning with a rational underpinning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites KSR and In re Kahn: Office personnel must provide a reasoned explanation as to why the invention would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention. Anti-patterns include conclusory statements and unsupported assertions that a combination 'would have been obvious.' Even when relying on common sense or ordinary ingenuity, the examiner must articulate the rationale (see Ball Aerosol and In re Van Os).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of applicant evidence; whole-record preponderance standard
rubrics_metrics.description: When an applicant properly submits evidence (in the specification, prior to a rejection, or in reply), the examiner must consider that evidence and make the patentability decision based on the entire record by a preponderance of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner must evaluate rebuttal evidence along with the facts supporting the conclusion of obviousness, and the legal standard requires the evidence supporting the rejection to be more convincing than opposing evidence (In re Oetiker; In re Eli Lilly). A decision to make or maintain a rejection must be based on consideration of all evidence, including applicant-submitted evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply Graham factual inquiries and make appropriate factual findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination of obviousness is dependent on the facts of each case and requires appropriate factual findings as explained in MPEP § 2141 and § 2143 (i.e., scope and content of the prior art, differences between the prior art and the claims, level of ordinary skill, and secondary considerations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel must make factual findings necessary to explain a conclusion of obviousness and analyze those findings to link them to the legal conclusion. If factual findings required by the Graham inquiries cannot be made, the chosen rationale cannot support obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationales that may support a conclusion of obviousness (overview)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court in KSR identified several rationales that can support obviousness; these rationales must provide a link between factual findings and the legal conclusion of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The listed rationales (A–G) are illustrative, not exhaustive. Any rationale used must provide appropriate factual findings and explanation. It is often the case that more than one line of reasoning may support a conclusion of obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results
rubrics_metrics.description: To reject a claim on this rationale, Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries and articulate (1)–(4):
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (1) a finding that the prior art included each claimed element (not necessarily in a single reference); (2) a finding that one of ordinary skill could have combined the elements by known methods and each element in combination performs the same function as separately; (3) a finding that one of ordinary skill would have recognized that the combination's results were predictable; and (4) any additional Graham-based findings necessary to explain obviousness. If any of these findings cannot be made, this rationale cannot be used. Example: Anderson’s-Black Rock shows combining known elements yielding predictable results; counterexample Adams shows that predictable results requirement is essential and that teaching away can render combination nonobvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness may be supported when one known element is simply substituted for another and the substitution yields predictable results to a person of ordinary skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner must articulate why the substitution would have been obvious/predictable and provide the factual basis tying the substitution to the claimed result. Must still satisfy Graham inquiries and provide a link between facts and legal conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a known technique to improve similar devices/methods/products in the same way
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying a known technique to improve similar technologies in the same manner can support obviousness if the improvement would have been predictable to one of ordinary skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel must explain why the technique would have been applied and why the resulting improvement would have been predictable, including necessary factual findings and any relevant examples or prior art teachings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying a known technique to a known device ready for improvement to yield predictable results
rubrics_metrics.description: If a known device is ready for improvement, applying a known technique to it such that the results are predictable can support obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must show the device was 'ready for improvement' and that applying the technique would predictably produce the claimed results. Provide factual findings linking prior art to the claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Obvious to try" — finite, predictable solutions with reasonable expectation of success
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Obvious to try' supports obviousness when there is a finite number of identified, predictable solutions and a person of ordinary skill would have had a reasonable expectation of success in trying them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner must show the problem and identified solutions were such that trying them would have been obvious and predictable. This rationale requires factual support that the solutions were limited and predictable rather than a vague or open-ended research program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictable variation from one field to another based on design incentives or market forces
rubrics_metrics.description: Known work in one field may prompt predictable variations for use in the same or a different field if design incentives or market forces would have made those variations predictable to one of ordinary skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show why the variations would have been predictable and how market/design incentives would have led a POSITA to make the variation; include factual findings linking the fields and motivations for variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching, suggestion, or motivation (TSM) in the prior art to modify or combine references
rubrics_metrics.description: Some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art that would have led a person of ordinary skill to modify or combine prior art teachings can support obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The TSM need not be an explicit statement in the prior art; however, the examiner must articulate why a POSITA would have been motivated to combine references or modify them, and must link factual findings to the legal conclusion. The court's requirement for an explicit analysis refers to the court's/examiner's reasoning, not necessarily to a recorded explicit teaching of motivation in the prior art (see Ball Aerosol).

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictability requirement and effect of teaching away
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining known prior art elements is insufficient to render a claimed invention obvious if the results would not have been predictable to one of ordinary skill; prior art that teaches away from a combination increases likelihood of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: United States v. Adams — although elements were known, prior art taught away and successful combination was nonobvious. Examiners must identify and evaluate any teachings away and cannot ignore teachings that would have deterred combination.
